  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic",

  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">New AI accelerators with novel instruction set architectures (ISAs) often require developers to manually craft low-level kernels — a time-consuming and error-prone process that does not scale across hardware targets. This delays emerging hardware platforms from reaching the market. While prior LLM-based code generation has shown promise in mature GPU ecosystems, it remains unclear whether agentic LLM systems can quickly produce valid and efficient kernels for emerging hardware with new ISAs. We present KernelCraft: the first benchmark for evaluating an LLM agent’s ability to generate and optimize low-level kernels for customized accelerators through a function-calling, feedback-driven workflow. We evaluate agent performance across three emerging accelerators on more than 20 machine-learning tasks, each with five diverse task configurations. Across four leading reasoning models, the strongest agents generate functionally correct kernels for unseen ISAs within a few refinement steps, and produce optimized kernels that match or outperform compiler baselines. These results demonstrate KernelCraft’s potential to accelerate the accelerator chip development cycle. KernelCraft is available at <a href="https://kernelcraft-cam.github.io/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://kernelcraft-cam.github.io/</a>.</p>

<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.ix1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">*</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.ix1.p1" class="ltx_para">

</div></li>

<p id="S1.I1.ix2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.ix2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Correct. = correctness; Perf. = performance; Code Sim. = code similarity (to a reference implementation).</span></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The rapid evolution of large language models (LLMs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al., 2023</a>)</cite> has necessitated a paradigm shift in AI accelerator design to accommodate increasingly complex computational patterns and memory bottlenecks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>. To maximize throughput and energy efficiency, emerging accelerators increasingly adopt specialized and heterogeneous instruction set architectures (ISAs), in contrast to the more general-purpose designs of conventional CPUs and GPUs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Unlike standard ISAs, these customized architectures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zeng et al., 2024</a>)</cite> expose low-level hardware abstractions, including computation patterns, data movement, and memory hierarchy, directly to the programmer. While this provides fine-grained control, it creates a “programmability wall”: most emerging accelerators lack the mature compiler toolchains required to automatically map high-level tensor programs to optimized bare-metal kernels. Building and maintaining a robust compiler stack for a customized accelerator with a new ISA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nigam et al., 2021</a>)</cite> requires substantial engineering effort. Therefore, this lack of a mature compiler creates a significant barrier to entry, often leaving innovative hardware underutilized or obsolete before it can be adopted by the AI community.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Existing machine learning compilers such as Apache TVM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2018</a>)</cite> aim to bridge this gap through automated kernel generation and optimization. However, adapting these frameworks to novel accelerators remains a “cold-start” problem, requiring engineers to manually encode hardware-specific constraints and memory hierarchies into the backend. As a result, translating high-level operator intent into close-to-metal kernel code continues to rely heavily on human expertise and careful reasoning about target-specific details, balancing functional correctness under hardware constraints with high performance through deep, hardware-specific tuning. This dependence makes kernel development time-consuming, error-prone, and difficult to scale, demanding deep expertise in both the target architecture and the computational workload. Consequently, even mathematically simple operators—such as linear layers, normalization, and attention—can require significant manual effort to implement efficiently, hindering the rapid iteration cycles for software-hardware co-design that is required by evolving AI workloads.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The rise of agentic systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Müller and Žunič, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Agarwal et al., 2020</a>)</cite> presents a solution to this human-centric implementation bottleneck. Recent work has explored leveraging LLMs to automate kernel generation with promising results for domain-specific languages, including Triton <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> and CUDA kernel optimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lange et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. However, these efforts largely target mature ecosystems with abundant training data and well-established programming patterns. As shown in <a href="#S1.T1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, these benchmarks fail to address the unique challenges of “zero-shot” kernel generation for emerging accelerators: In these scenarios, an effective agentic system must operate without prior programming examples, relying instead on the long-tail feedback from verification on hardware simulators and formal architectural specifications.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Hence, a critical question remains unanswered: <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Can agentic LLM systems quickly generate correct and close-to-metal kernel code for emerging hardware with novel instruction sets and architectural designs?</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">To address this gap, we propose <span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">KernelCraft</span>,
a tool-using agentic system that rapidly generates and optimizes high-performance low-level hardware kernels for customized accelerators with novel ISAs.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          Kernel correctness is non-trivial for emerging hardware. KernelCraft therefore integrates tool-based verification (e.g., compilation checks, simulation, and test-based validation) to detect functional errors during generation and optimization.</span></span></span> As illustrated in <a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, KernelCraft integrates an agentic execution loop with a systematic benchmark of workload specifications and hardware descriptions. The framework enables controlled evaluation and comparison of LLM agent capabilities across multiple emerging hardware platforms, providing a unified testbed for assessing functional correctness, optimization quality, and generalization to previously unseen ISAs.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2603.08721v2/fig2.png" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/269;" width="476" height="269" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S1.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">KernelCraft benchmarks LLM agents for accelerator assembly-kernel generation through a diagnosis-and-repair loop. Given workload, ISA, and hardware specifications, the agent writes an assembly kernel that KernelCraft automatically saves and verifies using syntax and reference-based functional checks. On mismatches, KernelCraft performs memory-level diff diagnostics and feeds the results back for iterative patching until the kernel satisfies correctness criteria.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Our contributions are as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce KernelCraft, the first benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on close-to-metal assembly kernel generation for emerging accelerators with novel ISAs, covering 33 tasks (23 ML, 10 CPU), six native tool interfaces, and diagnostic feedback across three emerging NPU platforms.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We demonstrate that frontier LLM agents can autonomously generate functionally correct bare-metal kernels for new instruction sets through limited iterative refinement, achieving an up to 56% success on primitive operations.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show that beyond correctness, agents can discover hardware-aware optimizations autonomously, generating kernels with competitive or superior performance.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We illustrate through case studies that KernelCraft extends naturally to broader hardware development workflows, from optimizing compiler templates to co-designing new instructions for emerging workloads.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>

<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Preliminaries</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Hardware kernel</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A hardware kernel is a low-level program that implements a specific computational task on a given hardware target, such as a customized AI accelerator or a general-purpose CPU.
In practice, hardware kernels may be expressed at different abstraction levels, ranging from high-level kernel languages or domain-specific languages (e.g., CUDA or Triton) to low-level representations such as intermediate code or assembly.
Regardless of the abstraction level, a hardware kernel ultimately specifies the computation, data movement, and control flow executed on the target hardware.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we focus on <em id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">ISA-level hardware kernels</em>, which are written directly in a hardware-specific instruction set architecture (ISA).
As a result, kernel correctness and performance are tightly coupled to the underlying ISA semantics and hardware constraints.
Such kernels consist of low-level scalar, vector, and memory-access instructions, rather than compiler intermediate representations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Tool-use-based LLM agents</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Tool use <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2025</a>)</cite> (also referred to as function calling) enables large language models to interact with external systems through predefined and structured interfaces (e.g., invoking external APIs or executing programs).
This paradigm has been widely adopted by modern LLMs, including DeepSeek <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and Qwen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, where the model selects appropriate functions based on user queries and outputs structured invocation arguments that are executed by the host application.
The execution results are then fed back to the model to support subsequent reasoning and response generation. By decoupling natural language reasoning from computation and external knowledge access, tool-use-based agents overcome several inherent limitations of standalone LLMs and serve as a foundation for contemporary agentic systems.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S2.T2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 2</span>: </span><span id="S2.T2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Tools Available in KernelCraft.<span id="S2.T2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Workload as input specifies the target task (e.g., linear, ffn, attention).</span></span></figcaption>

<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>KernelCraft</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">KernelCraft is an open-source benchmark designed to evaluate large language models for low-level assembly kernel generation on domain-specific accelerators.
It provides a unified framework for assessing model performance in generating correct and efficient bare-metal assembly code across a diverse set of accelerator architectures and workload complexities in an end-to-end workflow.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Each task in KernelCraft includes multiple variations, resulting in a large and diverse test space that stresses both correctness and performance across different execution contexts.
In addition, the benchmark natively supports multiple tools and execution backends, enabling agents to flexibly select and combine tools during kernel generation. <a href="#S1.F2" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows one example agent flow through this iterative loop, from the initial specifications to a correct kernel.</p>
</div>

<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Hardware targets.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider two classes of hardware targets in KernelCraft (<a href="#S3.T3" title="In 3.1 Hardware targets and kernel tasks ‣ 3 KernelCraft ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>): domain-specific AI accelerators (PLENA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, AMD NPU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">AMD, 2025</a>)</cite>, Coral NPU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google Research, 2025</a>)</cite>) and CPUs (e.g., the RISC-V–based Sonic BOOM core <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao and Gonzalez, 2020</a>)</cite>).
We select these systems to cover a diverse set of kernel development settings, ranging from fully customized accelerator ISAs with dedicated toolchains (PLENA and AMD NPU) to open-ISA targets built on RISC-V (Coral NPU and Sonic BOOM), which provide accessible documentation and widely used simulation frameworks. Each hardware target is described by its own ISA documentation and hardware specifications, which form the core of the agent’s system prompt, along with platform-specific tools (<a href="#S2.T2" title="In 2.2 Tool-use-based LLM agents ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). Full prompt structure is detailed in <a href="#A10" title="Appendix J KernelCraft System Prompt ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">J</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Kernel tasks.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We group ML- and CPU-related kernel generation tasks into three difficulty levels, based on increasing computational complexity and system integration, as summarized in <a href="#S3.T4" title="In Hardware targets. ‣ 3.1 Hardware targets and kernel tasks ‣ 3 KernelCraft ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and <a href="#S5.T10" title="In 5.2 Extending KernelCraft to the well-established ISA ‣ 5 Case Studies on KernelCraft Abilities ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>. All tasks target <em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">bare-metal kernels</em>: low-level implementations written directly against the target ISA or minimal compiler interfaces, where the kernel handles instruction selection, data movement, scheduling, and parallelism without high-level libraries or runtime abstractions. Level 1 covers primitive building blocks, including element-wise activations, normalization, linear algebra, spatial operators, and embedding lookups for AI accelerators, as well as arithmetic, memory, and basic linear algebra kernels for CPUs. Level 2 includes composite or algorithmic operations that combine primitives or require non-trivial control flow, such as MLPs, attention mechanisms, positional encoding, and loss functions on AI accelerators, and sorting or recursive algorithms on CPUs. Level 3 covers end-to-end workloads that integrate multiple operators, including complete Transformer and CNN blocks, along with synthetic and real-world applications and system-level CPU benchmarks.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Evaluation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our evaluation consists of two critical metrics on the generated kernels, namely <em id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">success rate</em> and <em id="S3.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">kernel performance</em>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the success rate, we consider a generation successful if the produced assembly kernel is functionally correct.
Correctness is verified by comparing kernel outputs against platform-specific ground-truth implementations under the target hardware semantics.
Because differences in instruction ordering, quantization, and accumulation can introduce numerical variation in assembly-level execution, exact equivalence with reference results is not always achievable.
We therefore apply tolerance-based validation, with platform-specific tolerance settings described in detail in <a href="#A3.SS2" title="C.2 Functional Correctness Checking Methods and Their Robustness ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Settings ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.2</span></a>.
A workload is deemed functionally valid if the generated output matches the reference within the specified tolerances.
We report success rates across five test cases with varying task configurations in <a href="#S3.T5" title="In Hardware targets. ‣ 3.1 Hardware targets and kernel tasks ‣ 3 KernelCraft ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For performance evaluation, we measure execution cycles via cycle-accurate simulation or on-device execution, depending on platform availability. Generated kernels are compared against compiler baselines from each platform’s standard toolchain (<a href="#A3.SS3" title="C.3 Kernel Generation Baseline ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Settings ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.3</span></a>). We report speedup as <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{B}{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mi>B</mi><mi>G</mi></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{B}{G}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G</annotation></semantics></math> denote the baseline and generated-kernel execution cycles or latency, respectively.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate KernelCraft across 3 accelerators and 4 frontier models with 5 configurations each, totaling over 1,100 experiments. We report success rates and kernel-level performance below; detailed experimental settings are provided in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Evaluation Settings ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Task success rate</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S3.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Hardware targets. ‣ 3.1 Hardware targets and kernel tasks ‣ 3 KernelCraft ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> shows a clear performance gap across models. GPT-5.2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2026a</a>)</cite> performs best on PLENA, AMD NPU, and Coral NPU, with success rates of 56%, 17%, and 47%, respectively. Gemini-3-Flash <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google, 2026</a>)</cite> ranks second, achieving 35%, 11%, and 39%. Sonnet 4 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2026</a>)</cite> and DeepSeek R1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> perform substantially worse; DeepSeek R1 generates only one successful kernel per platform.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Performance drops sharply as task complexity increases. Level 1 primitives achieve reasonable success rates, reaching 74% for GPT-5.2 on PLENA. However, Level 2 composite operations are substantially harder: GPT-5.2 drops to 45% on PLENA and below 10% on the other platforms. Level 3 end-to-end blocks remain largely unsolved, with only one successful ConvBlock kernel across all model–accelerator combinations, generated by Gemini-3-Flash on Coral NPU.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Success rates also differ significantly across accelerators. PLENA achieves the highest overall rates, while AMD NPU is the most challenging, remaining below 20% even for the best model. We partly attribute this gap to documentation quality: as shown in <a href="#S4.T6" title="In 4.1 Task success rate ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, PLENA’s system prompt is nearly 3<math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> longer than AMD NPU’s, mainly due to more extensive ISA documentation. We provide per-task and per-model token-usage breakdowns in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Token Usage Analysis ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>. Since Coral NPU does not officially support attention-based workloads, we evaluate it on a reduced task set; nevertheless, the same trend holds: higher task complexity strongly correlates with lower success rates across models and accelerators.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, these results show that KernelCraft captures a broad complexity spectrum in kernel generation. Due to cost constraints, we cap refinement at 15, 20, and 25 iterations for Levels 1–3, respectively. Despite these limits, the clear gradient from primitive to composite to end-to-end tasks suggests opportunities for improving agentic capabilities, such as in-context learning (Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Discussion ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>

<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Kernel performance</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.F3" title="In 4.1 Task success rate ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> presents a representative visualization of kernel-level speedups achieved by the best-performing KernelCraft agent on each task against each platform compiler. On PLENA, normalization tasks achieve consistent 1.06–1.22<math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedups across all configurations, while elementwise tasks degrade at larger scales. Coral NPU exhibits the largest gains, with speedups reaching 2–8<math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> on GEMV, GEMM, and ConvBlock. AMD NPU results cluster tightly around the baseline (0.89–1.18<math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>), with the most reliable improvements observed on GEMM and composite operations. Despite GPT-5.2 and Gemini-3-Flash demonstrating the highest task completion rates (Table <a href="#S3.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Hardware targets. ‣ 3.1 Hardware targets and kernel tasks ‣ 3 KernelCraft ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>), Gemini-3-Flash produces the most aggressively optimized kernels on Coral NPU—including the 7.93<math id="S4.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup on ConvBlock—suggesting that success rate and optimization quality are not perfectly correlated. These results indicate that <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">frontier models can generate both correct and performance-competitive kernels for novel ISAs</span>, though optimization quality varies significantly across operations, task complexity, and scale. Complete per-model cycle counts are provided in Tables <a href="#A5.T19" title="Table 19 ‣ Appendix E Workload Configurations and Performance Table ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a>, <a href="#A5.T21" title="Table 21 ‣ Appendix E Workload Configurations and Performance Table ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">21</span></a>, and <a href="#A5.T20" title="Table 20 ‣ Appendix E Workload Configurations and Performance Table ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">20</span></a> (Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Workload Configurations and Performance Table ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Discussion</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we outline a set of ablations intended to better understand the contribution of individual design choices and present key findings on agent-generated kernel behavior.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Extended reasoning is essential for hard kernel generation tasks.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Having identified the importance of extended thinking for successful kernel generation. We conducted an ablation study to quantify the impact of “thinking” tokens on task success, comparing standard inference against configurations with extended reasoning enabled. As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Extended reasoning is essential for hard kernel generation tasks. ‣ 4.3 Discussion ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, without extended thinking, GPT-5.2 fails to produce functional kernels within the iteration budget (0/5 success). Enabling reasoning tokens allows the agent to reason about hardware design and ISA implementation for Level 2 kernels, sustaining more iterations rather than terminating early. We selected moderate reasoning levels for each model as defaults across the main experiments to balance capability with cost; settings are documented in <a href="#A3.T14" title="In C.4 Models ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Settings ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>.</p>
</div>

Avg Iter: average iterations across 5 runs; Avg Tok: average tokens per iteration across 5 runs; Succ: success rate. Without thinking tokens, the model terminates early with 0% success. </section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">In-context learning is critical when ISA documentation is scarce.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We started out deliberately evaluating agents under a zero-shot setting across all accelerator platforms to assess their true ability to leverage tools and iteratively refine code on novel ISA specifications. Under this setting, agents struggle to produce correct kernels for complex, multi-operation tasks on PLENA and Coral. For the AMD NPU, where documentation is more limited, we provide a GEMM demonstration in the system prompt for the main experiments (<a href="#S3.T5" title="In Hardware targets. ‣ 3.1 Hardware targets and kernel tasks ‣ 3 KernelCraft ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To further quantify the impact of in-context learning, we conducted an ablation study (<a href="#S4.T8" title="In Extended reasoning is essential for hard kernel generation tasks. ‣ 4.3 Discussion ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>). Providing demonstrations of related workloads significantly improves success rates: GPT-5.2 improves from 1/5 to 4/5 on MQA kernels for PLENA with a Scaled Dot-Product example, and from 0/5 to 2/5 on AMD NPU FFN with a GEMM example. However, effectiveness remains model-dependent—Gemini 3 Flash shows minimal improvement across both platforms. These results suggest that curating reference implementations of foundational operations provides a strong basis for agentic kernel generation, enabling rapid adaptation to novel hardware and ever-increasingly complex ML workloads.</p>
</div>

<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Tool-use efficiency.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As summarized in Table <a href="#S1.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, existing work on agents for kernel generation typically does not leverage native tool use, instead employing external orchestration loops where the agent serves solely as a code generator while a separate system manages compilation, error checking, and feedback. Such designs require extensive prompt engineering, conflating model capabilities with surrounding infrastructure and making it difficult to evaluate inherent agentic abilities.
KernelCraft addresses this gap by relying solely on native API tool-use capabilities, directly measuring a model’s ability to autonomously handle coding writing through tool-calling interfaces.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate GPT-5.2, GPT-5.2 Chat <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2026b</a>)</cite>, Qwen3-Coder-Flash, DeepSeek-R1, and DeepSeek-V3.2. Notably, despite producing optimized CUDA kernels on KernelBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, DeepSeek-V3.2 and DeepSeek-R1 completely failed on KernelCraft.
Analysis of failure modes reveals fundamental deficiencies in tool use: DeepSeek-V3.2 returns <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">finish_reason="stop"</span> after the first <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">write_code</span> call, terminating the agentic loop before ever invoking <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">run_evaluation</span>.
We additionally compare GPT-5.2 against its chatbot variant, GPT-5.2 Chat, which fails to use tools entirely – outputting assembly code as plain text in its response rather than calling the <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">write_code</span> tool, leaving the code never saved or evaluated.
We demonstrate that tool-calling is a fundamental capability needed in KernelCraft for achieving good performance. More importantly, using tool-call enabled LLMs eliminate the need for carefully designed hand-crafted agentic loops like the ones in KernelBench.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Close-to-metal kernel generation enables optimizations absent from immature toolchains.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Agent-generated kernels can outperform compiler baselines by applying cross-operator optimizations that the target platform’s toolchain does not yet support.
For example, on the Coral NPU ConvBlock workload, the agent achieves up to a <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="7\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup.
The ConvBlock consists of a Conv2D followed by BatchNorm and ReLU, where activations and weights are quantized to int8 while BatchNorm parameters remain in floating point, reflecting realistic quantized inference settings.
In this setting, the compiler implementation incurs expensive float–int conversions inside the inner loop.
In contrast, the agent discovers BatchNorm folding by precomputing normalization parameters as fixed-point constants and fusing BatchNorm into integer arithmetic.
This eliminates all floating-point operations from the inner loop and yields a <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3.34\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.34</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.34\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup over the compiler baseline.
While such fusion passes are often absent from the immature toolchains of emerging accelerators, the agent can discover and apply them directly at the assembly level.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Documentation quality and harness design measurably contribute to kernel generation success.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Assembly generation for novel ISAs differs from standard code generation and requires task-specific support (Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Harness Ablation ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>). We quantify the impact of documentation, tooling, and prompting. Ablating the ISA documentation at three levels of detail (<a href="#A6.T22" title="In Appendix F Harness Ablation ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tables</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">22</span></a> and <a href="#A6.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Appendix F Harness Ablation ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>), we find that denser documentation consistently improves success, and that practical programming guidance is the most useful context for agents. Among the supporting files (<a href="#A6.T25" title="In Appendix F Harness Ablation ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">25</span></a>), the memory-layout document is by far the most critical across all four platforms. On BOOM, even removing the ISA specification has no effect on success rate (<a href="#A6.T26" title="In Appendix F Harness Ablation ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">26</span></a>), consistent with RISC-V being well represented in pretraining data. Tooling and prompting contribute comparably. <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">grep_docs</span> is the load-bearing tool (<a href="#A6.T23" title="In Appendix F Harness Ablation ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">23</span></a>): successful runs rely on it more as task complexity grows, whereas failed runs do not. Removing the KernelCraft prompts sharply degrades performance (<a href="#A6.T24" title="In Appendix F Harness Ablation ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">24</span></a>), and the two prompt components show opposite platform sensitivities.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Error Analysis.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We classify each failed run over the PLENA
(<a href="#A7.F9" title="In G.1 Error Analysis ‣ Appendix G Supplementary Analysis ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figures</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> and <a href="#A7.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ G.1 Error Analysis ‣ Appendix G Supplementary Analysis ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>) and Coral NPU
(<a href="#A7.F7" title="In G.1 Error Analysis ‣ Appendix G Supplementary Analysis ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figures</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> and <a href="#A7.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ G.1 Error Analysis ‣ Appendix G Supplementary Analysis ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>) logs into four
execution-failure categories (Syntax Error, Simulator Runtime Error, Timeout,
Tool Orchestration Error) and two functional-correctness categories (Low Accuracy,
Zero Match), and observe qualitatively different failure modes across platforms and
models. Syntax errors mainly arise from hallucinated opcodes unsupported by the target ISA. Timeouts concentrate on Coral at L2,
where models fall back to scalar operations instead of the RISC-V vector extension and
blow the cycle budget. Tool-orchestration errors are dominated by DeepSeek-R1, which
exhausts its output budget on planning without invoking <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">write_code</span>. These
patterns align with our tool-usage analysis
(<a href="#A7.F11" title="In G.2 Tool Usage Analysis ‣ Appendix G Supplementary Analysis ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figures</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>, <a href="#A7.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ G.2 Tool Usage Analysis ‣ Appendix G Supplementary Analysis ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> and <a href="#A7.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ G.2 Tool Usage Analysis ‣ Appendix G Supplementary Analysis ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>),
where successful runs invoke supporting tools more heavily as complexity grows. We refer
readers to Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Supplementary Analysis ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>, along with per-platform scaling behavior
(<a href="#A7.F14" title="In G.3 Scaling Analysis ‣ Appendix G Supplementary Analysis ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figures</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>, <a href="#A7.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ G.3 Scaling Analysis ‣ Appendix G Supplementary Analysis ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> and <a href="#A7.F16" title="Figure 16 ‣ G.3 Scaling Analysis ‣ Appendix G Supplementary Analysis ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>)
and per-workload ISA coverage
(<a href="#A7.T28" title="In G.4 Benchmark Design Analysis ‣ Appendix G Supplementary Analysis ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tables</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">28</span></a> and <a href="#A7.T29" title="Table 29 ‣ G.4 Benchmark Design Analysis ‣ Appendix G Supplementary Analysis ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">29</span></a>), for full details.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Case Studies on KernelCraft Abilities</h2>

<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Improving compiler templates</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond generating kernels from scratch, KernelCraft also demonstrates versatility in optimizing existing compiler templates. By incorporating hand-designed kernel templates into the system prompt, agents directly modify template logic while using the same tool-calling interface to evaluate assembly and iteratively refine performance. On the PLENA compiler’s FFN kernel template, the agent identifies that fully unrolled projection loops incur excessive scalar pointer arithmetic. It then leverages hardware loop instructions from the ISA specification and precomputes loop-invariant pointers to reduce overhead. For configuration C2 in <a href="#A5.T16" title="In Appendix E Workload Configurations and Performance Table ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>, the optimized template achieves a 94.5% reduction in instruction count and a 2.9% latency improvement by replacing repeated unrolled code with hardware loops and optimizing the tiling order. Appendix <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Case-study: Improving Compiler Template (FFN) for PLENA ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a> presents both the original and KernelCraft-optimized templates. These results show that KernelCraft can naturally extend beyond kernel generation to compiler development and optimization tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate the generality of KernelCraft beyond accelerator-oriented kernels, we extend our study to a diverse set of CPU workloads.
These benchmarks span primitive operations, algorithmic kernels, and end-to-end system workloads, with results summarized in <a href="#S5.T10" title="In 5.2 Extending KernelCraft to the well-established ISA ‣ 5 Case Studies on KernelCraft Abilities ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>.
Our results show that KernelCraft is able to generate kernels whose performance is comparable to that of well-established compiler toolchains in most cases.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Extending KernelCraft to GPUs</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further evaluate the generality of KernelCraft on NVIDIA’s Streaming Assembly (SASS). Since NVIDIA SASS is not publicly documented and varies across GPU generations, we leverage CuAssembler <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">cloudcores, 2024</a>)</cite>, an open-source PTX-to-SASS workflow, to extract instruction information, convert it into concise documentation, and integrate it into KernelCraft. We add a preliminary NVIDIA SASS experiment, shown in <a href="#A4.T15" title="In Appendix D Extending KernelCraft to GPUs ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> (Appendix  <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Extending KernelCraft to GPUs ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>), demonstrating that most models struggle to generate correct SASS under limited documentation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Competing with human expert-tuned kernels</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare the assembly code generated by KernelCraft with hand-written kernels for the Coral NPU development team, with results summarized in <a href="#S5.T11" title="In 5.4 Competing with human expert-tuned kernels ‣ 5 Case Studies on KernelCraft Abilities ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>.
The reference kernels are fully optimized for CNNs, with computation pipelines carefully scheduled and all execution stages explicitly fixed by human experts.
Our experimental results show that, while KernelCraft is able to generate a functionally correct kernel for this complex task within 15 iterations, its performance remains significantly lower than that of the fully optimized hand-tuned code.
This performance gap highlights both the difficulty of matching expert-level manual optimization and the opportunity for further improvement in automated kernel generation.</p>
</div>

<section id="S5.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.5 </span>Co-designing ISA for emerging ML workloads</h3>

<div id="S5.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">During our experiments, we observed an intriguing behavior: when agents encounter inefficiencies in the current ISA specification, they attempt to propose new instructions to address the gap. This motivated a case study to evaluate LLM agents as collaborators in ISA co-design for emerging workloads, specifically diffusion language models (dLLMs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nie et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ye et al., 2025</a>)</cite> on the PLENA accelerator.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Unlike autoregressive models, dLLMs perform iterative parallel denoising: in a typical setting, at each decoding step, the model predicts tokens across all masked positions, scores them by confidence, and selectively unmasks the highest-confidence predictions. This sampling pattern is not efficiently captured by the baseline PLENA ISA. To test the agent’s ability to independently identify architectural gaps, we intentionally withheld specialized instructions proposed in prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lou et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. By extending KernelCraft with a conversational mode for iterative human feedback, the agent independently identified the deficiency and proposed instructions that closely mirrored the human-expert ISA design. Once the human in the loop provided the held-out instruction descriptions in the conversation context, the agent successfully implemented the sampling kernel. These findings highlight the potential for an agent-assisted co-design flow, where agents not only implement kernels but also proactively identify and resolve the hardware bottlenecks. Appendix <a href="#A9" title="Appendix I KernelCraft Case-study: Co-Designing ISA for Emerging ML Workloads (dLLM) ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a> presents the entire case study.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We presented KernelCraft, the first benchmark for evaluating LLM agents’ ability to generate low-level assembly kernels for emerging AI accelerators with newly introduced ISAs.
Covering three complexity levels and multiple accelerator platforms, KernelCraft provides standardized tasks, tool interfaces, and diagnostic feedback to support fair comparisons of agent capabilities.
Evaluation of four frontier LLMs shows promising capabilities for generating effective kernels, but also reveals large performance gaps and several limitations. For example, some frontier models still struggle to complete end-to-end blocks, and exhibit a significant drop in performance for cases with insufficient documentation. Nonetheless, agent-generated kernels can match, and in some cases outperform, hand-optimized C++ implementations on the same hardware, while achieving up to <math id="S6.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup over compiler-generated baselines.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Future Work</h2>

<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Extension with formal verification.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Kernel correctness verification remains crucial yet unstandardized, for both LLM-generated code and existing toolchains. KernelCraft currently ensures functional correctness only through numerical validation. Future work could explore agents generating formal correctness proofs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Fusing ISA knowledge into models.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our BOOM case study shows that internalized ISA knowledge leads to notably strong performance, suggesting that future work could embed ISA specifications directly into model training or fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Agent system capabilities.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">KernelCraft could be extended with memory mechanisms that reduce per-iteration token usage, more specialized skill designs, and multi-agent settings.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Impact Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our work aims to facilitate the development of new AI accelerators. The direct impact is that it will speed up deployment. While the downstream technologies will then have other societal impacts, which should be considered carefully, our work will have only an indirect (enabling) effect. Hence, there is nothing else to highlight in this statement.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Benchmarks for Compute Kernel Generation</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In high-performance computing and deep learning systems, a compute kernel refers to a routine compiled for high-throughput accelerators (e.g., GPUs and NPUs) to perform specific mathematical operations. Unlike general-purpose software, such kernels require careful management of memory hierarchies and fine-grained thread parallelism.
Table <a href="#S1.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes existing benchmarks designed to evaluate LLMs on compute kernel generation tasks. KernelBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and TritonBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> assess LLMs’ capabilities in automatically generating GPU kernel code using CUDA and Triton, respectively. NPUEval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kalade and Schelle, 2025</a>)</cite> extends this evaluation to kernel generation for NPUs, while MultiKernelBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wen et al., 2025</a>)</cite> further broadens the scope by covering multiple hardware backends, including GPUs, NPUs, and TPUs.
In contrast, BackendBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saroufim et al., 2025</a>)</cite> focuses on evaluating PyTorch backend and kernel development, with a strong emphasis on production-level correctness and performance validation through PyTorch’s native testing infrastructure, rather than on standalone kernel code generation for specific accelerator programming models.
However, none of the above benchmarks are designed for custom accelerators. Our KernelCraft bridges this gap by benchmarking LLMs on generating low-level assembly code for kernel construction on custom accelerator architectures.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>LLM for Code Generation</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in code generation tasks, having been trained on large public and private code corpora. This is exemplified by state-of-the-art models such as OpenAI’s GPT-5, Anthropic’s Claude-4.5-Opus, and open-source alternatives like Qwen-3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and DeepSeek-V3.2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In academia, researchers are seeking ways to further improve the performance of code generation with LLMs.
However, relying solely on single-pass generation often fails to address complex programming challenges.
Consequently, recent studies have shifted focus towards Code Agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dong et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, systems that empower LLMs with the ability to plan, debug, and interact with execution environments iteratively to solve intricate software engineering tasks.
A common paradigm is multi-turn refinement, where agents iteratively generate, execute, and repair code based on execution feedback.
In this paradigm, the agent generates code, executes it against a set of unit tests or a compiler, and utilizes the resulting error logs or execution traces to repair the code in subsequent turns. Prominent examples include Reflexion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shinn et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, which employs verbal reinforcement to help agents reflect on feedback and correct their reasoning, and Self-Debug <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which enables LLMs to autonomously identify and fix bugs by analyzing execution results and explaining the code line-by-line.
Building upon these iterative strategies, AlphaEvolve <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Novikov et al., 2025</a>)</cite> has explored evolutionary approaches to optimize the generation process further.
It introduces a framework where code generated by the LLM is rigorously assessed, and based on this feedback, the system utilizes evolutionary algorithms to iteratively refine the prompts.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond internal reasoning and prompt optimization, recent advancements also equip single agents with external tool-use capabilities to overcome the limitations of static parametric knowledge.
By integrating with compilers, interpreters, and retrieval systems, agents can verify intermediate logic and access up-to-date documentation.
For instance, Toolformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schick et al., 2023</a>)</cite> demonstrates the efficacy of self-supervised API usage, while frameworks such as Parsel <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zelikman et al., 2023</a>)</cite> enable agents to decompose complex algorithmic tasks into hierarchical function calls.
Complementary to these approaches, Easytool <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2025</a>)</cite> addresses a practical bottleneck in tool-augmented agents by transforming diverse and verbose tool documentations into concise and unified tool instructions, significantly reducing token consumption and improving tool-use performance.
Scaling tool-use capabilities to real-world software development, CodeAgent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> tackles repository-level code generation by integrating a comprehensive suite of tools spanning information retrieval, code navigation, and testing, enabling agents to manage complex dependencies and external documentation that single-pass models often overlook.
Pushing this paradigm further into dynamic environments, Voyager <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> introduces lifelong learning, where an agent continuously writes and executes code to explore a game world.
It leverages execution feedback not only for immediate debugging, but also to curate a library of reusable code skills.
This paradigm transforms the LLM from a passive text generator into an active problem solver that interacts with its environment to validate hypotheses and accumulate practical experience.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">While these single-agent frameworks equipped with refinement loops and external tools have shown promise, they often struggle with complex software engineering tasks due to limited context retention and the lack of diverse perspectives. To address these challenges, recent research has shifted towards Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), which simulate human development teams by assigning distinct roles to specialized agents. ChatDev <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qian et al., 2024</a>)</cite> pioneers this approach by modeling the software development lifecycle as a communicative chain, where agents act as CEOs, CTOs, and programmers to collaborate through a waterfall model. Building on this, MetaGPT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2024</a>)</cite> incorporates Standardized Operating Procedures (SOPs) into the collaboration, requiring agents to generate structured outputs like Product Requirement Documents (PRDs) and UML diagrams before coding, thereby reducing hallucination and enhancing architectural consistency. Furthermore, AgentCoder <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> refines the verification process by introducing a multi-agent loop specifically designed for competitive programming; it employs separate agents for coding and test-case generation, allowing for rigorous self-verification against synthesized tests. Collectively, these frameworks demonstrate that decomposing complex coding tasks into specialized, collaborative sub-tasks yields superior robustness and code quality compared to monolithic generation approaches.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Automatic Compute Kernel Generation</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Due to the excellent code generation ability of LLMs, recent work has explored using LLMs and agentic frameworks to automate compute kernel generation and optimization for hardware accelerators.
A number of approaches focus on GPU kernels written in CUDA, where LLMs are combined with verification, search, or evolutionary strategies to iteratively discover high-performance implementations.
For example, the AI CUDA Engineer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lange et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and EvoEngineer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> frameworks automate CUDA kernel generation and optimization, demonstrating that LLM-guided evolution can achieve substantial speedups over baseline PyTorch or hand-written kernels while maintaining correctness.
In a similar spirit, inference-time scaling is effective for kernel generation: NVIDIA engineers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> demonstrate that DeepSeek-R1, coupled with a verifier-driven closed-loop workflow, can automatically generate and refine optimized GPU attention kernels that outperform expert-designed implementations in several cases.
Beyond CUDA-centric pipelines, some work emphasizes portability and operator coverage across accelerator platforms.
TritorX <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hammond et al., 2025</a>)</cite> presents an agentic system for generating Triton-based PyTorch ATen kernels at scale, prioritizing correctness and generality across diverse operators, data types, and shapes, thereby enabling rapid construction of backends for emerging ML accelerators.
Complementary to direct kernel generation, AlphaEvolve <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Novikov et al., 2025</a>)</cite> demonstrates that LLM-based agents can optimize hardware accelerator kernels across multiple abstraction levels, ranging from kernel-level tiling heuristics to direct optimization of compiler-generated intermediate representations that encapsulate kernels, such as FlashAttention.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Recent agentic approaches frame kernel generation and optimization as a closed-loop process rather than one-shot code synthesis: models iteratively propose kernels, invoke tools such as compilation/execution/profiling, and use automated verification to reject incorrect candidates and guide further refinements <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lange et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Robust-kbench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lange et al., 2025</a>)</cite> couples such scaffolding with verifier-guided evolutionary refinement to translate PyTorch modules into faster CUDA implementations under a more rigorous evaluation setup.
NVIDIA engineers similarly demonstrate inference-time scaling in a closed-loop workflow that repeatedly generates and refines CUDA attention kernels <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>.
Astra <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2025</a>)</cite> explores multi-agent optimization starting from existing CUDA kernels, coordinating iterative edits with testing and profiling to improve performance while maintaining correctness.
Beyond CUDA as a programming model, GEAK <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> targets Triton and uses Reflexion-style feedback to produce efficient kernels evaluated on a dedicated benchmark suite.
Overall, these agentic systems remain largely GPU-centric; NPUEval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kalade and Schelle, 2025</a>)</cite> is a notable exception that targets non-GPU devices by benchmarking NPU-oriented, domain-specific C++ kernels with compiler/hardware feedback.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">While these approaches demonstrate the promise of LLMs for automatic kernel generation and optimization, they predominantly target established programming models (e.g., CUDA, Triton, or compiler IRs) and mainstream accelerator architectures.
In contrast, our KernelCraft focuses on low-level compute kernel generation for custom accelerators, pushing automatic kernel generation below CUDA and compiler IRs by benchmarking LLMs on directly producing assembly code.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
