<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Evaluation Settings </h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our evaluation consists of two stages: functional correctness checking and performance evaluation of generated assembly kernels.
For correctness checking, we verify whether the generated assembly code produces numerically correct results under the target hardware semantics.
This process includes random input data generation, preparation of execution environments, execution via simulation or on physical hardware, and result validation.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Random data generation is used to create input stimuli for each kernel, enabling systematic correctness verification.
For each target platform, we compile the generated assembly kernel together with the corresponding input data to produce an executable artifact suitable for simulation or hardware execution.
Kernels are then executed either using cycle-accurate or RTL-based simulators, or directly on physical hardware, depending on platform availability.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Result validation is performed by comparing the execution outputs against standard reference results.
For machine learning workloads, we use PyTorch as the reference implementation, feeding identical input stimuli and checking numerical equivalence between the reference outputs and the kernel outputs.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">After functional correctness is established, we conduct a performance evaluation.
We measure simulated cycle counts when using simulators, or record actual execution time when running on physical hardware.
Performance is reported by comparing the generated assembly kernels against compiler-generated baselines or other ground-truth implementations under identical configurations.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, we implement a unified and automated evaluation pipeline across all evaluated accelerators and CPUs.
The hardware-specific execution environments are detailed below.</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>Hardware Setup</h3>

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="A3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PLENA.<span id="footnote1a" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
                      <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote1a.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">1</span></span>
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                    <a href="https://github.com/AICrossSim/PLENA_Simulator.git" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">https://github.com/AICrossSim/PLENA_Simulator.git</a></span></span></span></span>
PLENA provides a dedicated transactional simulator that executes compiled assembly code together with an explicit memory layout specification.
Given an assembly kernel, the simulator models instruction execution and memory accesses to produce numerical outputs.
Kernel correctness is verified by comparing the simulated outputs against reference results produced by PyTorch using identical inputs.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AMD NPU.<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
                      <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">2</span></span>
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                    <a href="https://github.com/Xilinx/mlir-aie.git" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">https://github.com/Xilinx/mlir-aie.git</a></span></span></span></span>
The AMD NPU does not provide a publicly available cycle-accurate simulator.
Instead, we evaluate kernels on physical AMD NPU hardware accessed via the AMD Strix cluster on the Ryzen AI Cloud.
We use the Peano compiler as a backend for AMD NPU code generation. High-level PyTorch programs are first lowered through the MLIR-AIR compiler stack to produce low-level representations, which are then compiled by Peano into executable binaries. In addition, Peano can directly compile low-level assembly code into executable binaries. In our experiments, KernelCraft-generated assembly kernels are compiled using Peano, deployed to the AMD NPU, and executed on-device. Correctness is validated by comparing hardware execution outputs against standard reference results.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Coral NPU.<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
                      <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">3</span></span>
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                    <a href="https://github.com/google-coral/coralnpu.git" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">https://github.com/google-coral/coralnpu.git</a></span></span></span></span>
The Coral NPU provides an open-source hardware and software stack, including complete RTL descriptions and a cocotb- and Verilator-based RTL simulation framework.
We compile kernels to the Coral NPU ISA and evaluate them using RTL simulation, enabling both functional verification and cycle-level performance measurement.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">BOOM.<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
                      <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">4</span></span>
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                    <a href="https://github.com/riscv-boom/riscv-boom.git" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">https://github.com/riscv-boom/riscv-boom.git</a></span></span></span></span>
For CPU evaluation, we use the open-source RISC-V–based Sonic BOOM core.
C++ kernels are compiled using a RISC-V toolchain into assembly and executable binaries.
Execution and correctness are evaluated using the Verilator-based RTL simulation framework provided with BOOM.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>Functional Correctness Checking Methods and Their Robustness</h3>

<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Correctness is verified by comparing kernel outputs against reference implementations elementwise. We follow KernelBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> in using <span id="A3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">numpy.allclose</span> with tolerance parameters. Our tolerances are platform-specific because each target performs computation in a different arithmetic format:</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="A3.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A3.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PLENA.</span> Activations use BF16 in VRAM; weights use MXFP8 (E4M3, 8-bit shared scale per block of eight) in HBM. Matrix multiplications accumulate in FP32, but intermediate results are quantized to BF16 between stages, introducing rounding errors. For multi-stage operators (e.g., FFNs), accumulated rounding can deviate up to one mantissa step (<math id="A3.I2.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{-6}\approx 0.015" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.015</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{-6}\approx 0.015</annotation></semantics></math>). We use <math id="A3.I2.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{\text{abs}}=0.012" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mtext>abs</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.012</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{\text{abs}}=0.012</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A3.I2.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{\text{rel}}=0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mtext>rel</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{\text{rel}}=0.01</annotation></semantics></math>. Ground-truth outputs are computed in PyTorch with MX quantization simulation.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AMD NPU.</span> Operating in full BF16 precision, we use <span id="A3.I2.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">torch.allclose</span> defaults. Ground-truth outputs are computed in C++ with full precision.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Coral NPU.</span> Supporting only integer arithmetic at the time of writing with the latest Coral NPU repo (Coral NPU is an developing project), we require exact equivalence (<math id="A3.I2.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=0</annotation></semantics></math>). Workloads are implemented in C++ with int8 quantization.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To contextualise our tolerance choices against industry practice, we examine existing production-level toolchains. NVIDIA CUTLASS uses a symmetric reference for NVFP/MXFP error tolerance:</p><pre id="A3.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">
# For MXFP in CUTLASS, eps = 0.1, non-zero floor = 1.526e-5
|a - b|  &lt;  eps * (|a| + |b|)        (general case)
|a - b|  &lt;  eps * nonzero_floor      (near-zero case)
</pre>
<p id="A3.SS2.p3.3" class="ltx_p">Triton adopts <span id="A3.SS2.p3.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">torch.allclose</span> with <span id="A3.SS2.p3.3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">atol=1e-3</span> and <span id="A3.SS2.p3.3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">rtol=1e-3</span>
for MXFP GEMM kernels. We further test these two error tolerance mechanisms on KernelCraft’s PLENA GEMM kernel experiments and find that the generated kernels pass with negligible errors. As shown in <a href="#A3.T12" title="In C.2 Functional Correctness Checking Methods and Their Robustness ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Settings ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, the generated kernels pass under all three tolerance mechanisms (KernelCraft, CUTLASS, and Triton). We integrate these industry-standard metrics from CUTLASS and Triton into the KernelCraft evaluation system, giving future users the flexibility to select tolerance settings appropriate to their hardware platform.</p>
</div>

<div id="A3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Additionally, we conducted a systematic input robustness evaluation (<a href="#A3.T13" title="In C.2 Functional Correctness Checking Methods and Their Robustness ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Settings ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>) to directly address boundary and adversarial inputs. We tested three functionally correct PLENA kernels across 13 conditions spanning four categories: random seeds (5 seeds), operand magnitude scaling (±0.003, ±0.03, ±0.3), edge cases (all zeros, all ones, all negative), and extreme values (1% outliers at 20× magnitude, asymmetric operand scaling). All three kernels pass across all conditions, confirming robustness to input distribution shifts.</p>
</div>

<section id="A3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.3 </span>Kernel Generation Baseline</h3>

<div id="A3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use platform-specific reference implementations to establish ground-truth correctness:</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="A3.I3" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A3.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I3.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PLENA.</span> Ground-truth outputs are computed in PyTorch with MX quantization.
Generated kernels are compiled using PLENA’s template-based compiler and executed on the PLENA transactional simulator.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I3.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Coral NPU.</span> Workloads are implemented in C++ with int8 quantization.
Generated kernels are compiled and evaluated using a Verilator-based RTL simulation framework.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I3.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I3.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I3.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I3.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AMD NPU.</span> Ground-truth outputs are computed in C++ using full-precision arithmetic.
Generated kernels are compiled using AMD’s NPU compiler toolchain and executed on AMD NPU hardware.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>

<math id="A5.T18.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> = number of elements,

<math id="A5.T18.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\text{in}},h_{\text{out}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mtext>in</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\text{in}},h_{\text{out}}</annotation></semantics></math> = input/output features,
<math id="A5.T18.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> = spatial dimension (height = width),
<math id="A5.T18.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\text{in}},c_{\text{out}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>in</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\text{in}},c_{\text{out}}</annotation></semantics></math> = input/output channels,
<math id="A5.T18.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> = channels (depthwise),
<math id="A5.T18.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> = kernel size.
All operations use int8 quantization.</span></span></p></div></div>

<section id="A7" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Supplementary Analysis</h2>

<div id="A7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This appendix section collects additional analysis that complements the results in the main text, covering error breakdowns, tool-usage patterns, scaling behavior, and benchmark ISA coverage across platforms.</p>
</div>
<section id="A7.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.1 </span>Error Analysis</h3>

<div id="A7.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We classify every failed run into four execution-failure categories (Syntax Error,
Simulator Runtime Error, Timeout, Tool Orchestration Error) and two functional-correctness
categories (Low Accuracy, Zero Match), and report the breakdown by model and by
task-complexity level for both PLENA and Coral NPU.</p>
</div>

<section id="A7.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.2 </span>Tool Usage Analysis</h3>

<div id="A7.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report how frequently the agent invokes each harness tool, broken down by
task-complexity level and, for the per-task view, by whether the run ultimately
succeeded.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A7.F11" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2603.08721v2/images/tools_analysis/coral_tool_usage_by_level_all_model.png" id="A7.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/187;" width="476" height="187" alt="Refer to caption">

<section id="A7.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.4 </span>Benchmark Design Analysis</h3>

<div id="A7.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To justify the completeness of our benchmark, we introduce an <em id="A7.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">instruction coverage</em> metric that quantifies how comprehensively the selected workloads exercise ISA-level primitives. For each workload, the metric measures the fraction of each ISA extension invoked—spanning arithmetic, memory-access, vector, and control-flow instructions—together with the union across all workloads. <a href="#A7.T28" title="In G.4 Benchmark Design Analysis ‣ Appendix G Supplementary Analysis ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tables</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">28</span></a> and <a href="#A7.T29" title="Table 29 ‣ G.4 Benchmark Design Analysis ‣ Appendix G Supplementary Analysis ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">29</span></a> report this coverage for the RISC-V ISA in Coral NPU and the PLENA ISA, respectively. The selected tasks collectively exercise a broad spectrum of hardware-relevant operations, supporting the reliability and completeness of the benchmark.</p>
</div>

<section id="A9" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix I </span>KernelCraft Case-study: Co-Designing ISA for Emerging ML Workloads (dLLM)</h2>

<div id="A9.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section presents the agent trace for the ISA co-design case study described in <a href="#S5.SS5" title="5.5 Co-designing ISA for emerging ML workloads ‣ 5 Case Studies on KernelCraft Abilities ‣ KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-MetalKernel Generation on Emerging Hardware" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.5</span></a>. The agent is tasked with implementing a <span id="A9.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">get_transfer_index</span> kernel for diffusion language model (dLLM) sampling on the PLENA accelerator. We include the task specification and show how the agent identifies ISA gaps, proposes new instructions, and iteratively implements the kernel once the human expert provides the final instruction designs. The final kernel achieved 100% correctness at 14,201 ns latency. We use <span id="A9.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Gemini-3-Pro-Preview</span> with thinking level set to high.</p>
</div>

<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">Agent Identifying ISA Gaps</h3>

<div id="A9.SSx1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="A9.SSx1.p1.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="545.95" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 477.38 545.95" width="477.38"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,545.95) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#DAA520;" fill="#DAA520" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 4.63 L 0 541.32 C 0 543.87 2.07 545.95 4.63 545.95 L 472.75 545.95 C 475.3 545.95 477.38 543.87 477.38 541.32 L 477.38 4.63 C 477.38 2.07 475.3 0 472.75 0 L 4.63 0 C 2.07 0 0 2.07 0 4.63 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#FFF8DC;" fill="#FFF8DC" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0.69 4.63 L 0.69 510.77 L 476.68 510.77 L 476.68 4.63 C 476.68 2.45 474.92 0.69 472.75 0.69 L 4.63 0.69 C 2.45 0.69 0.69 2.45 0.69 4.63 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 12.93 517.82)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:30.64em;--ltx-fo-height:1.7em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.18em;font-size:10pt;" height="25.92" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 23.49)" width="423.97"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A9.SSx1.p1.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:30.64em;">
<span id="A9.SSx1.p1.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="A9.SSx1.p1.pic1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\triangleright" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;" mathcolor="#FFFFFF" mathsize="0.900em">⊳</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\triangleright</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A9.SSx1.p1.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;"> Agent Reasoning</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 12.93 10.16)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:32.63em;--ltx-fo-height:35.49em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="491.14" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 491.14)" width="451.51"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A9.SSx1.p1.pic1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:32.63em;">
<span id="A9.SSx1.p1.pic1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A9.SSx1.p1.pic1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">I’m tasked with generating assembly for a “Get Transfer Index” kernel on PLENA. This means finding the <span id="A9.SSx1.p1.pic1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">argmax</span> of some logits, calculating a confidence score via softmax, applying a mask, selecting the top-k confidence values, and updating tokens. […] The instruction set looks somewhat restrictive, and it looks like it lacks critical instructions for this particular workload.</span></span>
<span id="A9.SSx1.p1.pic1.2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A9.SSx1.p1.pic1.2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The heart of the challenge is in the logic. I need to iterate over tokens, compute the index of the max logit (that’s <span id="A9.SSx1.p1.pic1.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">argmax</span>), calculate the confidence score, apply the mask, and select the top-k indices. Here’s where the architectural limitations start to bite. The instruction set seems to lack instructions for finding the argmax, particularly in the context of vector operations. Finding the argmax without a vector comparison instruction (e.g., <span id="A9.SSx1.p1.pic1.2.2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">V_EQ</span>, <span id="A9.SSx1.p1.pic1.2.2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">V_GT</span>) presents a big hurdle, as I cannot extract index value to GP reg. Also, I cannot use INT_MEM directly to index into VRAM as there is no way to do it.</span></span>
<span id="A9.SSx1.p1.pic1.2.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A9.SSx1.p1.pic1.2.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">[…] I am essentially blocked by a lack of a mechanism to “read back” vector data into scalar registers to drive control flow or update memory. I can’t directly read from VRAM or FP register to make decisions or index into the <span id="A9.SSx1.p1.pic1.2.3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">INT_MEM</span>, which is how the tokens <span id="A9.SSx1.p1.pic1.2.3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">x</span> and <span id="A9.SSx1.p1.pic1.2.3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">x0</span> are stored.</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>

<span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The current ISA requires enhancements. I propose:</span></span>
<span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">1. <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">V_CMP_GT_VV_MASK gp_rd, v_rs1, v_rs2</span><span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> — Compare vector <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">rs1</span> with <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.2.1.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">rs2</span> element-wise. If <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.2.1.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">rs1[i] &gt; rs2[i]</span>, set bit <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.2.1.2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">i</span> in <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.2.1.2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gp_rd</span> to 1, otherwise 0. <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.2.1.2.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Use case: updating max_val and argmax_idx in the argmax loop.</span></span></span></span>
<span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">2. <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">V_TOPK_MASK v_rd, v_rs1, imm_k</span><span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> — Identifies the <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.3.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">k</span> largest elements in vector <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.3.1.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">rs1</span>. Writes 1.0 to <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.3.1.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">v_rd</span> at top-k positions, 0.0 elsewhere. <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.3.1.2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Use case: <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.3.1.2.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">transfer_index = top_k(confidence, k)</span>.</span></span></span></span>
<span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">3. <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">V_LD_INT v_rd, gp_rs1, imm</span><span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> — Load VLEN integers from INT_MEM, convert to BF16, store in VRAM. <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.4.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Use case: loading <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.4.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">x</span> and <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.4.1.2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">x0</span> tokens into VRAM for processing.</span></span></span></span>
<span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">4. <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">V_ST_INT v_rd, gp_rs1, imm</span><span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> — Store BF16 values from VRAM to INT_MEM as integers. <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.5.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Use case: storing updated <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.5.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">x</span> tokens back to INT_MEM.</span></span></span></span>
<span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.6" class="ltx_p"><span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">5. <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">V_AND_VV rd, rs1, rs2</span><span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> — Bitwise AND on two vectors. <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.6.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Use case: combining masks.</span></span></span></span>
<span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.7" class="ltx_p"><span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Planned implementation:<span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Loop 256 times (vocab). Use <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.7.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">V_CMP_GT_VV_MASK</span> to compare with running max, update both <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.7.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">max_val</span> and <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.7.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">argmax_idx</span>. Then softmax denominator loop, <span id="A9.SSx3.p1.pic1.2.7.1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">V_TOPK_MASK</span> on confidence, and final update via masked merge.</span></span></span>

<section id="A9.SSx4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">Conversation Mode: Providing Held-out Instruction Specifications</h3>

<div id="A9.SSx4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.SSx4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">After reviewing the agent’s proposals, the human expert appended the held-out instruction specifications to the conversation context. These instructions were designed independently by a hardware engineer and intentionally withheld during the initial agent interaction to test whether the agent could identify the architectural gaps on its own.</p>

<span id="A9.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A9.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The issue is with the inner loop using <span id="A9.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">C_LOOP_START</span>. The specified register is used by the <em id="A9.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">hardware</em> to track iterations. My manual increment of <span id="A9.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gp2</span> is fighting the hardware’s internal decrement—the register is being modified by two independent mechanisms, leading to the infinite loop. </span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>

<section id="A10" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix J </span>KernelCraft System Prompt</h2>

<div id="A10.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A10.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The KernelCraft agent system prompt follows a modular template structure composed of four components: (1) a shared base prompt across accelerators defining the agent’s role and workflow, (2) a tool specification appended inside the system prompt to emphasize available tools, (3) accelerator-specific content containing ISA and memory documentation, and (4) hardware-specific guidance with debugging strategies and common pitfalls. Components (1) and (2) are shared across all accelerators, while (3) and (4) are instantiated per backend.</p>
</div>
<section id="A10.SSx1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">Part 1: Shared Base Prompt</h3>

<div id="A10.SSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A10.SSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The shared prompt establishes the agent as an expert assembly code generator operating in an autonomous multi-turn tool-calling loop. It enforces a two-phase workflow: first achieving functional correctness, then optimizing for performance.</p>
</div>

<section id="A11" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix K </span>KernelCraft Example Entire Agent Trace: Scaled Dot-Product Attention Kernel Generation for PLENA</h2>

<div id="A11.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A11.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section provides a complete reasoning trace of an LLM agent generating an optimized Scaled Dot-Product Attention kernel for the PLENA accelerator. The trace illustrates the iterative refinement process, including debugging, correctness verification, and performance optimization. We include the workload specification in natural language and conclude with the final optimized kernel that achieved 100% correctness with an 11.3% latency reduction over its initial correct implementation.</p>

<span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Alright, the code is ready, time to thoroughly examine it. For <span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M_TMM</span>, the source registers are <span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">rs1=VRAM</span> and <span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">rs2=MSRAM</span> – perfect. The MSRAM address stride is 256, again, correct. Similarly, for <span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M_MM</span>, <span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">rs1=MSRAM</span> and <span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.2.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">rs2=VRAM</span> are accurate. The MSRAM address stride is 4. Yep, all good. The <span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.2.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M_MM_WO</span> address calculation, <span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.2.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">row_blk*256 + col_blk*4</span> is right.</span></span>
<span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Now, a small, but crucial detail: <span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M_TMM</span> accumulates. So, I must verify the accumulator is cleared before each block’s first <span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M_TMM</span>. Oh, wait! <span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M_MM_WO</span> clears the accumulator, so each <span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">col_blk</span> loop iteration starts with a clean slate.</span></span>
<span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Wait, did I forget to include the inner <span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">k_blk</span> loop? My code doesn’t have it. I need to be sure. Ah, that’s because <math id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">d</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">=</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d=64</annotation></semantics></math>, and <span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M_MM</span> and <span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M_TMM</span> work on <math id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="MLEN=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">E</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">N</mi></mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">=</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">MLEN=64</annotation></semantics></math> elements at a time. The code’s design processes a full summation over <math id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=0\dots 63" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">k</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">=</mo><mrow><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">0</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">63</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=0\dots 63</annotation></semantics></math> with just one <span id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.2.4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M_MM</span> call. But wait, is that true? Let’s confirm by reading the workload spec carefully. “Fetch a (BLEN, MLEN) tile from Vector SRAM … and a (MLEN, BLEN) tile from Matrix SRAM”. Yes, <math id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="BLEN=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">B</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">E</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">N</mi></mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">=</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">BLEN=4</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="MLEN=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">E</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">N</mi></mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">=</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">MLEN=64</annotation></semantics></math>. So, it computes <math id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(4,64)@(64,4)=(4,4)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">4</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">,</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">64</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">@</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">64</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">,</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">4</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">=</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">4</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">,</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">4</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(4,64)@(64,4)=(4,4)</annotation></semantics></math>. Exactly what is needed for one block of the score matrix! So, the loops over row and col blocks are set up correctly, and the <math id="A11.SSx2.p1.pic1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> loop…</span></span>

<span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Okay, here’s what I’ve got to sort through. <span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">First, let’s trace the scores computation. The code uses <span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M_TMM</span> which computes <math id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V@M^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">V</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">@</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">M</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V@M^{T}</annotation></semantics></math>. I have <math id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Q</mi><annotation <span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">I did, however, find a potential error in the memory address calculation for the <span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M_MM_WO</span> instruction. For the write address of <span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M_MM_WO</span>, the ISA says <span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec_base + i * MLEN</span> where <span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">i</span> goes from 0 to <span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">BLEN</span>. My destination for <span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.4.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">M_MM_WO</span> was <span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.4.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">4096 + row_blk*256 + col_blk*4</span>. Looking at the <span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.4.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MLEN</span> (64) and <span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.4.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">BLEN</span> (4) values, my write address calculation is correct in my row-major layout, since I am writing a block of 4 elements at addresses offset by 64.</span></span>
<span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">But, back to the softmax. I’m using the correct register operands in <span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">V_RED_MAX</span> and <span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">V_RED_SUM</span>. My row size is also correct, using the full <span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">VLEN</span> of 64 elements, which looks good. But, where’s the <span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">nan</span> coming from? It’s possible I need to apply <span id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.2.5.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">qk_scale</span> (0.125) before the max for numerical stability. My code calculates <math id="A11.SSx5.p1.pic1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S=QK^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">S</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">=</mo><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">Q</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">K</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">T</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S=QK^{T}</annotation></semantics></math>, then…</span></span>

<span id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Okay, wait a minute! <span id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Right, I’m multiplying <span id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">row_blk</span> by 64, then multiplying that result by 4. So <span id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gp13</span> should eventually equal <span id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">row_blk * 256</span>. Now, <math id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="row\_blk" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">w</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">_</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">row\_blk</annotation></semantics></math> ranges from 0 to 15, meaning the maximum value is <math id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="15\times 256=3840" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">15</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" lspace="0.222em" mathcolor="#000000" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">256</mn></mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">=</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">3840</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15\times 256=3840</annotation></semantics></math>. Okay, that’s within the expected bounds.</span></span>
<span id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.6" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">I was momentarily thrown off because <span id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S_MUL_INT</span> doesn’t take immediate values directly, so I had to use <span id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S_ADDI_INT</span> to load the constants.</span></span>
<span id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.7" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Let’s break it down:
<span id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gp13 = row_blk * 64</span>
<span id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gp13 = gp13 * 4</span> which does indeed give me <span id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.7.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">row_blk * 256</span>.</span></span>
<span id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.8" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.8.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Is <span id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">row_blk * 256</span> the correct offset for this? Each row block is 4 rows, and each row has 64 elements. So, 4 rows * 64 elements/row gives me 256 elements, exactly. Therefore, <span id="A11.SSx6.p1.pic1.2.8.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">row_blk * 256</span> correctly gives me the starting offset of that block. That’s good.</span></span>

<span id="A11.SSx7.p1.pic1.2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx7.p1.pic1.2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Okay, 100% match, that’s excellent. Now the real work begins: optimization! Let’s see… current latency is sitting at 42376 nanoseconds. Time to get this number down.</span></span>
<span id="A11.SSx7.p1.pic1.2.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx7.p1.pic1.2.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">My first thought is always instruction reduction. Let’s look at those loops. I see some immediate opportunities. Those multiplications:</span></span>
<span id="A11.SSx7.p1.pic1.2.4" class="ltx_listing ltx_lstlisting ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle ltx_listing" style="--ltx-border-color:#B3B3B3;"><span class="ltx_listing_data"><a href="data:text/plain;base64,U19BRERJX0lOVCBncDEsIGdwMCwgMjU2ClNfTVVMX0lOVCBncDExLCBncDcsIGdwMQ==" download="">⬇</a></span>
<span id="lstnumberx552" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx552.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">S_ADDI_INT</span><span id="lstnumberx552.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx552.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">gp1</span><span id="lstnumberx552.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">,</span><span id="lstnumberx552.5" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx552.6" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">gp0</span><span id="lstnumberx552.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">,</span><span id="lstnumberx552.8" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx552.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">256</span>
</span>
<span id="lstnumberx553" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx553.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">S_MUL_INT</span><span id="lstnumberx553.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx553.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">gp11</span><span id="lstnumberx553.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">,</span><span id="lstnumberx553.5" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx553.6" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">gp7</span><span id="lstnumberx553.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">,</span><span id="lstnumberx553.8" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx553.9" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">gp1</span>
</span>
</span>
<span id="A11.SSx7.p1.pic1.2.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx7.p1.pic1.2.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">can be done with incrementing. We’ll precalculate that outside the loop.</span></span>
<span id="A11.SSx7.p1.pic1.2.6" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx7.p1.pic1.2.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Next, prefetching! Can we get ahead of the game with loading data? Specifically, can we prefetch the <math id="A11.SSx7.p1.pic1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> matrix? The memory model is usually <span id="A11.SSx7.p1.pic1.2.6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MLEN <math id="A11.SSx7.p1.pic1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> MLEN <math id="A11.SSx7.p1.pic1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 4</span>, with <span id="A11.SSx7.p1.pic1.2.6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MLEN</span> being 64, so that’s 4096 elements per tile. The ISA tells us how the matrix tiles are addressed sequentially. Let’s see… the matrix SRAM can hold at least 4 tiles, with the layout specified. <math id="A11.SSx7.p1.pic1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> is currently in tile zero, so we can prefetch <math id="A11.SSx7.p1.pic1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> to address 4096.</span></span>
<span id="A11.SSx7.p1.pic1.2.7" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx7.p1.pic1.2.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Finally, loop overhead. We could try combining the loops, but the 2D tiling is already pretty efficient, so I am not too worried about this. The priority is definitely in optimizing the address calculations, I will start there.</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>

<span id="A11.SSx11.p1.pic1.2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx11.p1.pic1.2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Okay, so I’ve managed to shave off some latency, bringing it down from 42376 ns to 37573 ns – roughly an 11% improvement. <span id="A11.SSx11.p1.pic1.2.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx11.p1.pic1.2.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">I’m thinking, if I can get V loaded <span id="A11.SSx11.p1.pic1.2.3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">before</span> that softmax loop kicks off, we might see another boost. <span id="A11.SSx11.p1.pic1.2.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx11.p1.pic1.2.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The plan is to use that <span id="A11.SSx11.p1.pic1.2.4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">H_PREFETCH_M</span> instruction. <span id="A11.SSx13.p1.pic1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx13.p1.pic1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Reflections on Optimization Results<span id="A11.SSx13.p1.pic1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span></span></span>
<span id="A11.SSx13.p1.pic1.2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx13.p1.pic1.2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Okay, so the latency has stayed exactly the same at 37573 ns. Interesting. This means one of two things is happening. Either the <span id="A11.SSx13.p1.pic1.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">H_PREFETCH_M</span> operation for <math id="A11.SSx13.p1.pic1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> is taking significantly less time than the softmax computation, so its latency was already masked by the bigger operation, or the prefetch engine and the compute engine in the simulator aren’t perfectly overlapping in <span id="A11.SSx13.p1.pic1.2.2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">this</span> particular instance.</span></span>
<span id="A11.SSx13.p1.pic1.2.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx13.p1.pic1.2.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">However, a 100% match rate and an improvement in latency compared to the baseline is a win, so I’m happy with that outcome. But, as always, my mind is still ticking, wondering if there are any further gains to be made.</span></span>
<span id="A11.SSx13.p1.pic1.2.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A11.SSx13.p1.pic1.2.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Let’s see… within the softmax loop, could we unroll it a little bit? But I should pause there for a moment. Given that the vector units are already being fully utilized with a VLEN of 64, this might not be possible. The current code <span id="A11.SSx13.p1.pic1.2.4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">is</span> quite clean and efficient. I don’t think I can improve the performance by optimizing the softmax loop.</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
